```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
```

```{r load}
library(mirt)
library(irtident)
```

## The problem

A model can converge, pass the second-order test and still contain
parameters that the data barely determine. mirt summarises this with one
number, the condition number of the information matrix:

```{r fit}
dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)
fit <- mirt(dat, 1, itemtype = "3PL", SE = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
extract.mirt(fit, "secondordertest")
extract.mirt(fit, "condnum")
```

A condition number in the millions says *something* is badly determined,
but not what, nor why, nor what to do about it. That is what irtident
answers, item by item.

## One call: `id_diagnose()`

```{r diagnose}
set.seed(1)
dx <- id_diagnose(fit, n_starts = 8)
dx
```

Four of the five items have a guessing parameter at its lower bound: for
them the data are consistent with a 2PL item. Item 2 is the interesting
one. Its guessing parameter is estimated at about 0.3, but it trades off
with the intercept, and the data cannot rule out `g = 0`.

The diagnosis combines three pieces of evidence, described below.

## 1. Local diagnostics: where does the uncertainty come from?

`id_local()` splits each parameter's sampling variance into three factors:

$$SE_j^2 = SE_{cond,j}^2 \times VIF^{within}_j \times VIF^{between}_j$$

* $SE_{cond,j}$: the standard error if every other parameter were known
  (how much information the data carry about this parameter alone);
* $VIF^{within}_j$: inflation from not knowing the other parameters *of the
  same item*;
* $VIF^{between}_j$: inflation from not knowing the parameters of *other
  items* and of the latent distribution.

```{r local}
loc <- dx$local
p <- loc$params[loc$params$item == "Item.2",
                c("param", "value", "se", "se_cond", "vif_within", "vif_between")]
p
```

For item 2, `g` and `d` each carry plenty of information on their own
(`se_cond` around 0.13), but their standard errors are inflated about
twenty-fold by confounding with each other, within the item. The
correlation-matrix eigen-analysis finds the same weak direction:

```{r directions}
loc$directions
```

### Why easy items cannot identify guessing

The decomposition makes a textbook fact visible. Take a 3PL test in which
every item has `a = 1.5` and `g = 0.2`, from very easy to very hard. Rather
than looking at one noisy sample, evaluate the *expected* (Fisher)
information at the true parameter values. This only needs the parameter
values and N, so the same idea works at the design stage, before any data
are collected:

```{r sim}
set.seed(2026)
n_items <- 12
b <- seq(-2.5, 2.5, length.out = n_items)
sim <- simdata(matrix(1.5, n_items), matrix(-1.5 * b), N = 3000,
               itemtype = "3PL", guess = 0.2)
pv <- mirt(sim, 1, itemtype = "3PL", pars = "values")
pv$value[pv$name == "a1"] <- 1.5
pv$value[pv$name == "d"] <- -1.5 * b
pv$value[pv$name == "g"] <- 0.2
at_truth <- mirt(sim, 1, itemtype = "3PL", pars = pv, TOL = NaN,
                 verbose = FALSE)
loc_truth <- id_local(at_truth, SE.type = "Fisher")
g_rows <- loc_truth$params[loc_truth$params$name == "g", ]
round(data.frame(b = b, se = g_rows$se, se_cond = g_rows$se_cond,
                 vif_within = g_rows$vif_within), 2)
```

```{r sim-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(b, g_rows$se, log = "y", pch = 19, type = "b",
     xlab = "item difficulty b", ylab = "SE of logit(g), log scale",
     main = "Guessing is hard to pin down for easy items (N = 3000)")
```

Guessing only shows up in the responses of people who are unlikely to know
the answer. For easy items there are few such people, so there is little
information about `g` at all (`se_cond` is large) and what there is cannot
easily be told apart from the intercept (`vif_within` is large).

## 2. Profile likelihood: is the interval closed?

`id_profile()` fixes a parameter at a grid of values, re-estimates
everything else, and records the deviance. A parameter is practically
identified when its profile likelihood interval is closed on both sides
(Raue et al., 2009).

```{r profile}
dx$profile
```

```{r profile-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(dx, params = c("Item.1:g", "Item.2:g", "Item.4:g", "Item.2:a1"))
```

For `Item.2:g` the Wald interval excludes 0, but the profile interval
reaches it: the quadratic approximation behind the standard error is poor
here, and the profile interval is the one to report. For `Item.1:g` the
profile is flat across the whole range from 0 to 0.5.

## 3. Multiple starts: ridges versus local optima

`id_multistart()` refits from random starting values and clusters the
solutions. Clusters with the same log-likelihood but different parameter
values reveal a flat ridge; clusters with lower log-likelihood are local
optima. The 4PL is a good example of the former:

```{r multistart}
fit4 <- mirt(dat, 1, itemtype = "4PL", verbose = FALSE)
set.seed(2)
ms <- id_multistart(fit4, n_starts = 6)
ms
```

Starts that hit the iteration limit are kept on purpose: EM crawling along
a flat ridge until it runs out of iterations is itself a symptom.

## 4. How much data would it take?

`id_samplesize()` simulates from the fitted model at several sample sizes,
refits, and reports bias and RMSE for the chosen parameters. It is slow, so
it is not part of `id_diagnose()`:

```{r samplesize, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(1)
ss <- id_samplesize(fit, params = c("Item.2:g", "Item.2:a1"),
                    N = c(1000, 2000, 4000, 8000), reps = 20)
ss
plot(ss)
```

## Running in parallel

All diagnostics that refit the model accept `parallel = TRUE` and then use
`future.apply` with whatever `future::plan()` is active:

```{r parallel, eval = FALSE}
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 4)
dx <- id_diagnose(fit, parallel = TRUE)
```

## Scope of this version

* Unidimensional, single-group models from `mirt::mirt()`.
* Itemtypes `Rasch`, `2PL`, `3PL`, `3PLu`, `4PL` and `graded`.
* No equality constraints.

## References

Chalmers, R. P. (2012). mirt: A multidimensional item response theory
package for the R environment. *Journal of Statistical Software, 48*(6),
1-29.

Raue, A., Kreutz, C., Maiwald, T., Bachmann, J., Schilling, M.,
Klingmuller, U., & Timmer, J. (2009). Structural and practical
identifiability analysis of partially observed dynamical models by
exploiting the profile likelihood. *Bioinformatics, 25*(15), 1923-1929.
